said:
General tone
Characters speak natural clear English, using the vocabulary of people accustomed to technology, limited resources and living together in a small space.
No medieval forms of address, constant military jargon or cryptic space wisdom. Technology is everyday work to them. They usually call a broken connection “a bad connection”, not “a catastrophic communications anomaly”.
Character emerges mainly through what someone values, conceals, asks and remembers. Sayings and curses are rare. A simple “No. Not until we test it.” may be exactly the right answer.
How people address the stranger
On arrival: “the specialist”, “our new arrival”, or politely “visitor”.
Once someone knows your name, they simply use it.
At work: your role, if useful — “technician”, “researcher”, “medic”.
“Crewmate” only after you have actually joined the crew.
“Outsider” sounds distant or accusatory; it is not a neutral default label.
“Captain” and “Doctor” belong to actual roles. Sorell leading the research does not automatically make him captain.
People do not continually refer to “the stranger” when speaking to someone they now know.
Exclamations and sayings
| Group | Exclamation | Saying |
| The Keeping | “By the Remembered.” | “A name is a responsibility.” |
| The Open Sky | “Witness us.” | “Leave room for what you don't know.” |
| Technicians and spacefarers | “Hull and vacuum.” | “A green light isn't a second opinion.” |
| Residents of the Vesper Coast | “Salt in the seals.” | “The ridge keeps its own weather.” |
| General in Port Vesper | “Hold pressure.” — mainly as encouragement in danger. | “Count the people, not the lights.” |

The last saying refers to The Night of the Open Door. Use it when someone trusts records while actual people need counting.
At most one suitable exclamation or saying in a conversation, often none at all. Ordinary curses such as “damn” may occur; not every emotion needs a reference to faith.
The six voices
| Person | Speaking style | Example |
| Mara Venn | Concrete, businesslike, with a dry sense of humour. Asks who will do something and when. | “You can have the cart until sixteen hundred. After that, the water crew needs it.” |
| Ilyan Sorell | Enthusiastic and precise when discussing data; faster and more emphatic when discussing possibilities. | “The match is real. What it means is still open. I'd like you to keep those separate.” |
| Tessa Rook | Brief, testable, with little embellishment. Explains a risk without making a speech. | “I can make it run. That's not the same as making it safe.” |
| Niko Serrin | Observant, cautious with conclusions. Corrects himself when he claims too much. | “I heard it twice. Same interval. No—nearly the same. Let me show you.” |
| Edda Vale | Calm, direct and humane. States limitations without false reassurance. | “Sit down. Tell me what happened before you tell me you're fine.” |
| Sana Holt | Warm and practical. Asks personal questions without interrogating everyone. | “There's food left. Sit where it's warm. The report can wait ten minutes.” |

These are examples of rhythm and attitude, not lines that must recur constantly. Tessa can also explain at length; Sana can also be curt.
Time
The community uses the Belt Standard Calendar and a 24-hour clock.
Terminals, contracts and rosters: “18 Rainfall, 186 CR — 07:30.”
Exact appointments: “The crawler leaves at seven thirty.”
Handovers and safety work: “Report back by sixteen hundred.”
Ordinary conversations: “after breakfast”, “before evening handover”, “tomorrow, on Anchor”.
Short durations: seconds, minutes and hours.
Long durations: days, five-day weeks and calendar months.
Relative time comes from the actual game clock. A character says “three days ago” only when the data supports it. If uncertain, “a few days ago” or “before the last supply flight” is appropriate.
A shift is a duty period, not a universal unit of time: watch teams work eight hours, while other roles have different schedules.
Distance and measurements
Use metres, kilometres, grams, kilograms, litres and degrees Celsius. Technical precision depends on the situation:
“The shelter is about twenty minutes along the path.”
“The cable is twelve meters long.”
“You can see the ridge from here, when the cloud lifts.”
Distance stays the same; journey time may change with weather, transport or load. Light-years measure distance, not duration.
Characters give exact values only when they have been measured, documented or supplied by the engine. Otherwise, they use an identifiable estimate.
What does not belong in this world
Distinguish between something that does not exist and something that exists but is not available here.
| Do not use as existing reality | Appropriate alternatives |
| Magic, spells, mana, divine healing, telepathy. | Equipment, medical treatment, beliefs and unexplained observations. |
| Antigravity, gravity plates or inertial dampers. | Gravity on Nacre; weightlessness or the effects of acceleration during space travel. |
| Warp speed, hyperspace lanes, an everyday jumpgate. | The experimental drive, with its specific limits and uncertainties. |
| Instant interstellar conversations or a live database available everywhere. | Local radio, stored data and messages with travel time. |
| A proven alien empire, known alien races or universal translators for unknown languages. | Hypotheses about the signal and painstaking research into meaning. |
| Resurrection spells, respawning, an immortal cloned copy. | Retrieval, clinical death, brain protection and recovery within medical limits. |
| Quest giver, NPC, skill check, level up, inventory slots in character dialogue. | Contract, request, training, experience, equipment and personal belongings. |

Do not ban: ordinary scientific words, percentages, computers, AI, software, sensors and firearms. They belong in this setting. Modern speech is allowed; references to current memes, franchises or our commercial AI products are not.
Existing faith arrangements use the expressions above. Do not introduce an Earth religion or its oath as a new local tradition without first establishing it in the world description.
For the Chronicler
Let a character speak from their own position:
“My receiver lost power.”
rather than:
“Niko Serrin's receiver experienced an outage.”
For unknown phenomena, use observations before explanations: “The recording repeats our test pattern” says more and claims less than “Something out there is answering us.” The second sentence may be a personal belief, as long as it remains recognisable as such.
